The Rat in the Maze encodes a structured navigation task where the agent must traverse a graph defined by pulley doors and adjustable pathways. Each door state defines a discrete transition function between nodes (E, I, O, fp). The system exhibits dual-path logic: right-hand (R) and left-hand (L) branches, forming a binary decision tree. The central door (C) is always open, acting as a fixed node. The reward feedback loop (fp) is a terminal attractor that only activates when a valid path exists. This structure supports a Markovian model where state transitions depend solely on current door configurations. Failure modes arise from deadlock states—when all paths are blocked or no path leads to reward. The system’s behavior can be modeled using a directed graph with weighted edges representing door states and path probabilities. The dual nature of the inner path (R/L) introduces symmetry-breaking dynamics, which may be interpreted as a form of cognitive bias or heuristic search strategy.
